questions.question_text: With respect to resonance structures of $\text{CO}_{3}^{2-}$ ion, which of the following statements are correct? (a) All $\text{C}-\text{O}$ bonds in $\text{CO}_{3}^{2-}$ are equivalent (b) There are three resonance structures possible for $\text{CO}_{3}^{2-}$ ion (c) The position of carbon and oxygen should change in every resonance structure (d) The formal charge on carbon atom is $-2$
questions.question_html:
With respect to resonance structures of $\text{CO}_{3}^{2-}$ ion, which of the following statements are correct?
(a) All $\text{C}-\text{O}$ bonds in $\text{CO}_{3}^{2-}$ are equivalent
(b) There are three resonance structures possible for $\text{CO}_{3}^{2-}$ ion
(c) The position of carbon and oxygen should change in every resonance structure
(d) The formal charge on carbon atom is $-2$

options.label: A
options.html: a, b and c

options.label: B
options.html: a and b only

options.label: C
options.html: b and d only

options.label: D
options.html: a, b and d

questions.explanation_text: In the carbonate ion, $\text{CO}_{3}^{2-}$ , carbon is at the centre and the three oxygen atoms are attached to it. The ion has three possible resonance structures. In each structure, one $\text{C}=\text{O}$ double bond and two $\text{C}-\text{O}^{-}$ single bonds are shown. The double bond can be placed with any one of the three oxygen atoms. So statement (b) is correct. In resonance, the actual structure is not any one of these structures. The actual carbonate ion is a resonance hybrid. Because of this, all three $\text{C}-\text{O}$ bonds become equivalent. Each $\text{C}-\text{O}$ bond has the same bond length and same bond strength, intermediate between a single bond and a double bond. So statement (a) is also correct. Statement (c) is incorrect because in resonance structures, the positions of atoms do not change. Only the positions of electrons, such as $\pi$ electrons and lone pairs, change. Statement (d) is also incorrect. The formal charge on carbon in carbonate ion is $0$ , not $-2$ . Using the formula, $\text{Formal charge}=\text{valence electrons}-\text{non-bonding electrons}-\frac{1}{2}(\text{bonding electrons})$ For carbon in $\text{CO}_{3}^{2-}$ , $\text{Formal charge on C}=4-0-\frac{8}{2}$ $=4-4=0$ Hence, the correct statements are (a) and (b) only . $\text{Option B}$
questions.explanation_html:
In the carbonate ion, $\text{CO}_{3}^{2-}$ , carbon is at the centre and the three oxygen atoms are attached to it.

The ion has three possible resonance structures. In each structure, one $\text{C}=\text{O}$ double bond and two $\text{C}-\text{O}^{-}$ single bonds are shown. The double bond can be placed with any one of the three oxygen atoms.

So statement (b) is correct.

In resonance, the actual structure is not any one of these structures. The actual carbonate ion is a resonance hybrid. Because of this, all three $\text{C}-\text{O}$ bonds become equivalent.

Each $\text{C}-\text{O}$ bond has the same bond length and same bond strength, intermediate between a single bond and a double bond.

So statement (a) is also correct.

Statement (c) is incorrect because in resonance structures, the positions of atoms do not change. Only the positions of electrons, such as $\pi$ electrons and lone pairs, change.

Statement (d) is also incorrect. The formal charge on carbon in carbonate ion is $0$ , not $-2$ .

Using the formula,

$\text{Formal charge}=\text{valence electrons}-\text{non-bonding electrons}-\frac{1}{2}(\text{bonding electrons})$

For carbon in $\text{CO}_{3}^{2-}$ ,

$\text{Formal charge on C}=4-0-\frac{8}{2}$

$=4-4=0$

Hence, the correct statements are (a) and (b) only.

$\text{Option B}$
key_concepts: Dipole Moment, Formal Charge & Hydrogen Bonding

questions.question_text: In which of the following option/options, the order of arrangement does not agree with the variation of property indicated against it? (a) $\text{BF}_{3}>\text{NF}_{3}>\text{NH}_{3}$ (Dipole moment) (b) $\text{HgCl}_{2}>\text{NH}_{4}^{+}>\text{SF}_{6}$ (Bond angle) (c) $\text{NH}_{3}<\text{H}_{2}\text{O}<\text{HF}$ (Strength of intermolecular hydrogen bonding) (d) $\text{H}-\text{I}>\text{H}-\text{Br}>\text{H}-\text{Cl}$ (Bond length)
questions.question_html:
In which of the following option/options, the order of arrangement does not agree with the variation of property indicated against it?
(a) $\text{BF}_{3}>\text{NF}_{3}>\text{NH}_{3}$ (Dipole moment)
(b) $\text{HgCl}_{2}>\text{NH}_{4}^{+}>\text{SF}_{6}$ (Bond angle)
(c) $\text{NH}_{3}<\text{H}_{2}\text{O}<\text{HF}$ (Strength of intermolecular hydrogen bonding)
(d) $\text{H}-\text{I}>\text{H}-\text{Br}>\text{H}-\text{Cl}$ (Bond length)

options.label: A
options.html: a, b and c

options.label: C
options.html: c and d only

questions.explanation_text: The arrangement which does not agree with the property is only (a) . For dipole moment: $\text{BF}_{3}$ is trigonal planar and symmetrical. The three $\text{B-F}$ bond dipoles cancel one another, so its dipole moment is $\mu(\text{BF}_{3})=0$ $\text{NF}_{3}$ is pyramidal, so it has some dipole moment, but it is small because the bond dipoles oppose the lone pair effect. $\text{NH}_{3}$ is also pyramidal, and its dipole moment is greater than that of $\text{NF}_{3}$ . So the correct order is $\text{NH}_{3}>\text{NF}_{3}>\text{BF}_{3}$ But the given order is $\text{BF}_{3}>\text{NF}_{3}>\text{NH}_{3}$ So (a) is incorrect. Now checking the others: In (b), $\text{HgCl}_{2}=180^{\circ},\text{NH}_{4}^{+}=109.5^{\circ},\text{SF}_{6}=90^{\circ}$ So $\text{HgCl}_{2}>\text{NH}_{4}^{+}>\text{SF}_{6}$ is correct. In (c), hydrogen bonding strength increases with electronegativity of the atom attached to hydrogen: $\text{N}<\text{O}<\text{F}$ So $\text{NH}_{3}<\text{H}_{2}\text{O}<\text{HF}$ is correct. In (d), bond length increases with the size of halogen atom: $\text{Cl}<\text{Br}<\text{I}$ So $\text{H-I}>\text{H-Br}>\text{H-Cl}$ is also correct. Hence, the correct option is: $\text{Option B: a only}$
questions.explanation_html:
The arrangement which does not agree with the property is only (a).

For dipole moment:

$\text{BF}_{3}$ is trigonal planar and symmetrical. The three $\text{B-F}$ bond dipoles cancel one another, so its dipole moment is

$\mu(\text{BF}_{3})=0$

$\text{NF}_{3}$ is pyramidal, so it has some dipole moment, but it is small because the bond dipoles oppose the lone pair effect.

$\text{NH}_{3}$ is also pyramidal, and its dipole moment is greater than that of $\text{NF}_{3}$ .

So the correct order is

$\text{NH}_{3}>\text{NF}_{3}>\text{BF}_{3}$

But the given order is

$\text{BF}_{3}>\text{NF}_{3}>\text{NH}_{3}$

So (a) is incorrect.

Now checking the others:

In (b),

$\text{HgCl}_{2}=180^{\circ},\text{NH}_{4}^{+}=109.5^{\circ},\text{SF}_{6}=90^{\circ}$

So

$\text{HgCl}_{2}>\text{NH}_{4}^{+}>\text{SF}_{6}$

is correct.

In (c), hydrogen bonding strength increases with electronegativity of the atom attached to hydrogen:

$\text{N}<\text{O}<\text{F}$

So

$\text{NH}_{3}<\text{H}_{2}\text{O}<\text{HF}$

is correct.

In (d), bond length increases with the size of halogen atom:

$\text{Cl}<\text{Br}<\text{I}$

So

$\text{H-I}>\text{H-Br}>\text{H-Cl}$

is also correct.

Hence, the correct option is:

$\text{Option B: a only}$
key_concepts: Dipole Moment, Formal Charge & Hydrogen Bonding

questions.question_text: The types of hybrid orbitals of nitrogen in $\text{NO}_{2}^{+},\text{NO}_{3}^{-}$ and $\text{NH}_{4}^{+}$ respectively are
questions.question_html: The types of hybrid orbitals of nitrogen in $\text{NO}_{2}^{+},\text{NO}_{3}^{-}$ and $\text{NH}_{4}^{+}$ respectively are
questions.explanation_text: For finding the hybridisation of nitrogen, we count the number of electron domains around nitrogen. Electron domains include: sigma bonds lone pairs For $\text{NO}_{2}^{+}$ : Nitrogen is bonded to two oxygen atoms. Structure is: $\text{O}=\text{N}=\text{O}$ Nitrogen has 2 sigma bonds and no lone pair. So, steric number: $2+0=2$ Steric number $2$ means linear shape and $sp$ hybridisation. So, nitrogen in $\text{NO}_{2}^{+}$ is $sp$ hybridised. For $\text{NO}_{3}^{-}$ : Nitrogen is bonded to three oxygen atoms. Due to resonance, all three $\text{N-O}$ bonds are equivalent. Nitrogen has 3 sigma bonds and no lone pair. So, steric number: $3+0=3$ Steric number $3$ means trigonal planar shape and $sp^{2}$ hybridisation. So, nitrogen in $\text{NO}_{3}^{-}$ is $sp^{2}$ hybridised. For $\text{NH}_{4}^{+}$ : Nitrogen is bonded to four hydrogen atoms. Nitrogen has 4 sigma bonds and no lone pair. So, steric number: $4+0=4$ Steric number $4$ means tetrahedral shape and $sp^{3}$ hybridisation. So, nitrogen in $\text{NH}_{4}^{+}$ is $sp^{3}$ hybridised. Hence, the hybridisations are: $\text{NO}_{2}^{+}:sp,\text{NO}_{3}^{-}:sp^{2},\text{NH}_{4}^{+}:sp^{3}$ Correct option: Option B $sp,sp^{2},sp^{3}$
questions.explanation_html:
For finding the hybridisation of nitrogen, we count the number of electron domains around nitrogen.

Electron domains include:

  • sigma bonds

  • lone pairs

For $\text{NO}_{2}^{+}$ :

Nitrogen is bonded to two oxygen atoms.

Structure is:

$\text{O}=\text{N}=\text{O}$

Nitrogen has 2 sigma bonds and no lone pair.

So, steric number:

$2+0=2$

Steric number $2$ means linear shape and $sp$ hybridisation.

So, nitrogen in $\text{NO}_{2}^{+}$ is $sp$ hybridised.

For $\text{NO}_{3}^{-}$ :

Nitrogen is bonded to three oxygen atoms. Due to resonance, all three $\text{N-O}$ bonds are equivalent.

Nitrogen has 3 sigma bonds and no lone pair.

So, steric number:

$3+0=3$

Steric number $3$ means trigonal planar shape and $sp^{2}$ hybridisation.

So, nitrogen in $\text{NO}_{3}^{-}$ is $sp^{2}$ hybridised.

For $\text{NH}_{4}^{+}$ :

Nitrogen is bonded to four hydrogen atoms.

Nitrogen has 4 sigma bonds and no lone pair.

So, steric number:

$4+0=4$

Steric number $4$ means tetrahedral shape and $sp^{3}$ hybridisation.

So, nitrogen in $\text{NH}_{4}^{+}$ is $sp^{3}$ hybridised.

Hence, the hybridisations are:

$\text{NO}_{2}^{+}:sp,\text{NO}_{3}^{-}:sp^{2},\text{NH}_{4}^{+}:sp^{3}$

Correct option: Option B

$sp,sp^{2},sp^{3}$

questions.explanation_text: The electronic configurations of elements $X$ and $Y$ are as follows: $X:1s^{2}2s^{2}2p^{6}3s^{2}3p^{3}$ $Y:1s^{2}2s^{2}2p^{6}3s^{2}3p^{5}$ For element $X$ , the configuration corresponds to phosphorus (P), which is in group 15 of the periodic table. For element $Y$ , the configuration corresponds to chlorine (Cl), which is in group 17. Phosphorus ( $P$ ) has a valency of 3 or 5. Chlorine ( $Cl$ ) has a valency of 1. Given these valencies, possible compounds could form: $PCl_{3}$ , where phosphorus uses its valency of 3 to bond with three chlorine atoms. $PCl_{5}$ , where phosphorus uses an expanded valency of 5 to bond with five chlorine atoms. Both $PCl_{3}$ and $PCl_{5}$ are covalent compounds. In both scenarios, sharing of electrons occurs between phosphorus and chlorine atoms, resulting in covalent bonds.

questions.explanation_text: To calculate bond order, we use the formula: $\text{Bond order}=\frac{1}{2}(\text{number of bonding electrons}-\text{number of antibonding electrons})$ Here's how the bond order is calculated for each molecule/ion: For the NO molecule: $\text{BO}=\frac{1}{2}(8-3)=2.5$ For the CO molecule: $\text{BO}=\frac{1}{2}(10-4)=3.0$ For the $\text{O}_{2}^{-}$ ion: $\text{BO}=\frac{1}{2}(6-3)=1.5$ For the $\text{O}_{2}$ molecule: $\text{BO}=\frac{1}{2}(6-2)=2.0$
questions.explanation_html:
To calculate bond order, we use the formula:

$\text{Bond order}=\frac{1}{2}(\text{number of bonding electrons}-\text{number of antibonding electrons})$

Here's how the bond order is calculated for each molecule/ion:

For the NO molecule:

$\text{BO}=\frac{1}{2}(8-3)=2.5$

For the CO molecule:

$\text{BO}=\frac{1}{2}(10-4)=3.0$

$\text{BO}=\frac{1}{2}(6-3)=1.5$

For the $\text{O}_{2}$ molecule:

$\text{BO}=\frac{1}{2}(6-2)=2.0$

questions.question_html: Bond enthalpies of $A_{2},B_{2}$ and $AB$ are in the ratio $2:1:2$ . If bond enthalpy of formation of $AB$ is $-100kJmol^{-1}$ . The bond enthalpy of $B_{2}$ is
questions.explanation_text: Given, $(BE)_{A_{2}}:(BE)_{B_{2}}:(BE)_{AB}=2:1:2$ where, $BE=$ Bond enthalpy $(\Delta H_{f})_{AB}=-100kJ$ Let the $BE$ of $A_{2},B_{2}$ and $AB$ be $2x,x$ and $2x$ respectively. As we know, $\Delta_{f}H^{\circ}=\Sigma\Delta_{\text{diss}}H_{R}^{\circ}-\Sigma\Delta_{\text{diss}}H_{P}^{\circ}$ where, $\Delta_{\text{diss}}H^{\circ}=$ Enthalpy of dissociation $\begin{aligned} \frac{1}{2}A_{2} & +\frac{1}{2}B_{2} \rightarrow AB \\ \therefore -100 & =(\frac{1}{2}2x+\frac{1}{2}x)-x \\ x & =200 \end{aligned}$ $\therefore$ Bond enthalpy of $B_{2}$ is $200kJmol^{-1}$ .
questions.explanation_html:
Given,

$(BE)_{A_{2}}:(BE)_{B_{2}}:(BE)_{AB}=2:1:2$

where, $BE=$ Bond enthalpy

$(\Delta H_{f})_{AB}=-100kJ$

Let the $BE$ of $A_{2},B_{2}$ and $AB$ be $2x,x$ and $2x$ respectively.

As we know, $\Delta_{f}H^{\circ}=\Sigma\Delta_{\text{diss}}H_{R}^{\circ}-\Sigma\Delta_{\text{diss}}H_{P}^{\circ}$

where, $\Delta_{\text{diss}}H^{\circ}=$ Enthalpy of dissociation

$\begin{aligned} \frac{1}{2}A_{2} & +\frac{1}{2}B_{2} \rightarrow AB \\ \therefore -100 & =(\frac{1}{2}2x+\frac{1}{2}x)-x \\ x & =200 \end{aligned}$

$\therefore$ Bond enthalpy of $B_{2}$ is $200kJmol^{-1}$ .
